Title: Diagnosis
Details:
- What the failing test does
  - testLargeSample builds polynomials of degree 0..9 and, for each, creates a PolynomialFitter with a Levenberg–Marquardt optimizer.
  - It then adds 40,000 observed data points (weights all equal to 1.0) and calls fit with an initial guess to recover the coefficients.

- Call chain and where the problem happens
  - PolynomialFitter.fit(double[]) simply delegates to CurveFitter.fit with a Parametric model.
  - CurveFitter.fit(int, T, double[]), at lines 156–178, builds:
    - target: a double[] of length n = observations.size().
    - weights: a double[] of length n (from each WeightedObservedPoint’s weight).
    - It then calls optimizer.optimize(..., new Target(target), new Weight(weights), new InitialGuess(initialGuess)).
  - The creation of new Weight(weights) is the critical step.

- Why it fails for large samples
  - The bug report states: “When using the Weight class to pass a large number of weights to multivariate vector optimizers, an n×n full matrix is created (and copied) when a n elements vector is used. This exhausts memory when n is large.”
  - In this test, n = 40,000; forming an explicit n×n dense matrix for weights means allocating on the order of 1.6 billion doubles (~12.8 GB), which is infeasible in typical test environments.
  - As a result, the optimizer invocation tries to allocate (and even copy) this massive matrix (and possibly more during subsequent computations), leading to out-of-memory or similar resource exhaustion, causing the test to fail before it can verify accuracy.

- Evidence tie-in
  - CurveFitter.fit builds the weights[] vector and passes it to the new Weight(weights) object.
  - The bug report precisely describes that the new multivariate vector optimizers (used here via org.apache.commons.math3.optim.nonlinear.vector.jacobian.LevenbergMarquardtOptimizer) mishandle the weights vector by expanding it to a dense matrix internally.
  - The failure only manifests with “large number of points,” which matches both the test (40,000 points) and the report (e.g., 4,120 points observed by the reporter).

- Root cause
  - The Weight(double[]) path (and/or the consuming optimizer code) expands the diagonal weight vector into a full dense matrix and subsequently copies it, causing prohibitive memory usage for large n.
  - The code should treat weights as a diagonal operator (or use a specialized diagonal/linear-operator representation), and avoid materializing a dense n×n matrix.
